title: Lens Inquiry: An Astronomy Lab for Non-science Majors at Hartnell Community College
extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and implementation of a three-hour inquiry-based astronomy lab activity centered on converging lenses and telescopes. The authors focus on replacing a more guided laboratory exercise with an inquiry format in which students generate their own questions, design investigations, discuss observations, and present results to the class. The paper is primarily concerned with instructional design and classroom implementation rather than with testing a specific AI or digital intervention.

The activity was implemented in a semester-long astronomy laboratory course for non-science majors at Hartnell Community College, a Hispanic-serving institution in Salinas, California. Students worked in small groups of 2-4, first exploring lens phenomena through demonstrations and guided question generation, then selecting a question to investigate, making posters, and presenting findings. The lesson concluded with a telescope-building worksheet and synthesis segment connecting lens properties to telescope design.

The authors report that the activity was effective at promoting communication, peer interaction, and engagement with scientific inquiry, but they also note that it was difficult to cover all desired content within the available time. They conclude that the lab would likely work better if split into two sessions and that more facilitation time and tighter limits on materials and possible investigations would improve future implementations. The paper provides formative and summative assessment observations, including a final-exam item on converging lenses, but does not present a controlled comparison study of outcomes.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed conference paper describing a classroom intervention, but it is primarily a qualitative design/implementation report rather than a controlled evaluation. No experimental comparison group, effect size, or rigorous causal design is reported.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests positive classroom engagement and some content understanding, but the evidence is descriptive and based on a small community-college sample rather than a measured medium/large effect. The reported 58% correct on one exam item is informative but not enough to establish strong impact.

finding.finding_summary: The inquiry lab was designed to build scientific process skills, including planning investigations, controlling variables, and communicating findings. The paper reports qualitative success in these areas, but also notes that some groups reached premature conclusions and did not revise them despite contradictory evidence; on a final exam conceptual item about converging lenses, 58% answered correctly, which the authors describe as close to the class average for the lab final.
finding.measure: Observation of inquiry process skills; group poster/presentation rubrics; final exam question on converging lenses

finding.finding_summary: A major goal of the activity was to strengthen communication, collaboration, and confidence through group investigations and short presentations. The authors report that students were generally relaxed during presentations, engaged in active class discussions, and the activity helped students get to know classmates better; these were descriptive findings rather than quantified effects.
finding.measure: Classroom observations; student feedback/comments; presentation participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on astronomy content learning about converging lenses and simple telescope construction rather than a core K-12 subject area. Students completed a telescope worksheet and a conceptual final-exam item, and the authors report that 58% answered the lens question correctly, suggesting some content uptake despite time constraints.
finding.measure: Telescope worksheet; final exam conceptual question on converging lenses
